title: Half-Hour Paper Splice — Context Shifts & Practical Notes
content:
Goal: short, actionable synth of a few recent reads — what to try in the next sprint, quick eval ideas, and questions to bring to the weekly kv-cache sync. This is a scratchpad: half-hour reads + my immediate takeaways (hence 'splice').

Topline impressions:
- Trend: papers increasingly treat KV cache not as passive memory but as an active, mutable data structure (sharding, eviction policies, compressed indices). There are recurring themes: locality-aware eviction, cheap delta updates for long sessions, and token-alignment for compressed caches.
- Practical gap: many works assume clean evals (synthetic contexts or single-domain dialogues). We need small, robust probes that reflect real Redwood traffic: multi-domain chat sessions with retrieval hits, noisy user edits, and rapid topic switches.

Papers skimmed (30m each) + one-line takeaways:
1) Sparse-Aware KV Sharding (arXiv:2601.01234) — takeaway: shard by semantic clusters instead of fixed token ranges; reduces remote fetches for multi-topic sessions. Implementation note: try sharding by embedding-clusters from our existing retrieval embeddings (reuse compute). Risk: cluster drift across sessions — need periodic reassign or lightweight bloom filter per-shard.
2) Quant-Stable Attention (internal draft) — takeaway: low-bit quant can break attention head norms subtly; authors propose tiny per-head scale corrections learned on small calibration sets. Implementation note: add per-head affine correction hooks in our quant pipeline and test on the small calibration suite (5k prompts) before rollout.
3) Prefix-Compact Caching (blog+code) — takeaway: compress repeated prefixes with run-length style pointers + lightweight decompression on hot paths. Implementation note: benchmark memory vs CPU trade-offs: for short-chat workloads compression may be net-negative because of decompression overhead; but for long-window retrieval-heavy apps it's promising.

Concrete experiments to run (next 2 sprints):
- Experiment A: "Clustered-Shard KV" prototype. Steps: (1) build a pipeline to compute per-session chunk embeddings (reuse embeddings service), (2) run k-means (k~32) to create shard assignments, (3) serve a local simulation that routes cache lookups to shard replicas and measure remote fetch rate and end-to-end latency on recorded sessions. Success metric: >=20% fewer remote fetches without >5% latency regression. Links: see linked_artifacts PR for proto.
- Experiment B: "Per-Head Quant Correction". Steps: instrument quant pipeline to collect per-head activation stats, apply affine correction during dequant, run 1k eval prompts measuring PPL and safety/regression metrics. Success metric: <1% increase in token error vs full precision while saving target memory.
- Experiment C: "Prefix Compact vs No-Compact" microbench. Use synthetic long-document sessions + a sample of 500 real user sessions. Measure CPU overhead and peak memory. Decide: enable only for workloads with >X tokens/session.

Evaluation and probes (quick ideas):
- Build a small 'fragile case' probe set: sessions that intentionally flip topic, include retrieval noise, and user truncation—these often trigger worst-case fetch patterns.
- Add a small A/B harness to Redwood Console dashboard: per-session remote_fetch_rate, mean_lookup_time, and fallback rate. Surface regressions with automatic alerting threshold (e.g., +10% fetch rate).

Open questions / doubts:
- How stable are embedding-clusters across time? If clusters drift fast, clustered-shard approach could require heavy maintenance. Possible mitigation: incremental reclustering or LSH hash-stable shards.
- Does per-head affine correction generalize to new models or only the family we tested? Might need model-specific calibration hooks in the platform.
- Are there security/privacy implications to storing compressed prefix pointers? If prefix compression uses pointers into other session data, must ensure isolation for private deployments.

Notes to self / followups:
- Ping Iris to get the 2026-05 session logs sample (5M tokens) for Experiment A simulation.
- Drop a short note in #serving-runtime about adding a tiny hook in quant pipeline for per-head correction metrics.
- Draft a 1-pager for the product team outlining how prefix compression could be toggled per-tenant (Dedicated vs Hosted) with simple heuristics.

Quick glossary (for this scratchpad):
- shard: KV cache partition that can be colocated or remote.
- clustered-shard: shard assignment based on embedding clusters rather than fixed token index.
- per-head correction: tiny learned scale/shift applied to dequantized attention head outputs to compensate quantization bias.

Final micro-reflection: half-hour splices work well for surfacing actionable ideas. Keep this format for quick sprint planning — a couple high-level experiments, a short eval plan, and explicit fail-criteria.

End of note.
